civilopediaText.text: Infantry regiments and brigades of about 3,000 men. They took and held the ground, and in the hedgerows they did almost all the fighting.
Parachute and glider infantry: lightly armed, but picked, superbly trained and used to fighting surrounded.

Tanks, assault guns and tank destroyers. Fast and powerful in the open fields around Caen; blind and vulnerable in the hedgerows, woods and towns, where an enemy with an anti-tank gun or a Panzerfaust could wait unseen a few yards away: -20% in rough terrain.
Towed anti-tank guns: deadly when dug in and waiting for tanks, poor in the attack (-25%).
Field artillery battalions and regiments. Unlike the guns of earlier wars they fired from behind cover at targets their forward observers could see, so most of them fire over obstacles.
Towed guns must Set Up before firing. Self-propelled guns and rocket launchers need not.
Coast-defence batteries in concrete casemates. They cannot move.

Battleships, cruisers and destroyers of the bombarding forces. Naval gunfire was the Allies' heavy artillery on D-Day and for weeks afterwards: it could reach well inland, and German commanders came to dread it.
Corps and division commanders with their staffs. They inspire nearby troops but cannot fight, and they are lost if the enemy reaches them.
Supply columns and medical units: non-combatants that keep the army supplied and its wounded alive.
